summary: RFCs contain fixed elements such as the title page header, standard boilerplates and copyright statements. This informational RFC describes them and updates them to reflect current practice, to show clearly the source of RFC creation and review. It obsoletes RFC 5741.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for the cover page and fine print of every RFC, including who made it and how it was reviewed.

subtitle: The fixed cover-page header and Status of This Memo text that tell readers which stream an RFC came from and how it was reviewed.

tldr.problem: Readers could confuse RFCs that went through the IETF's review with RFCs that had a very different review and approval process.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC title page header names the originating stream, and the Status of This Memo has three paragraphs that state the status, the review the document received, and where to find updates. The exact wording lives on an IAB web page.
tldr.outcome: This RFC obsoletes RFC 5741 and has itself been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920.

facts.label: Categories
facts.value: Standards Track, Best Current Practice, Experimental, Informational, Historic

today: RFC 7841 is an Informational RFC published in May 2016 that obsoletes RFC 5741. It has since been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920, and the exact boilerplate wording is kept on an IAB web page rather than in the RFC.

sections.title: Why RFCs Carry Boilerplate
sections.content:
RFCs contain fixed elements that exist for historical, practical and legal reasons: the title page header, standard boilerplate text and copyright and intellectual property statements. As the RFC Series evolved there was growing concern about labeling each RFC clearly. The chief requirement is that RFCs published as part of the IETF's review process must not be easily confused with RFCs that may have had a very different review and approval process.

This memo identifies and describes the common elements of RFC boilerplate structure and the content each kind of information must contain. It leaves the exact text and layout to a web page maintained by the IAB, so that details are easy to maintain. It obsoletes RFC 5741, moving detailed content to that web page and preparing for more flexible output formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Some papers look official but were checked very differently. The fine print on the cover page makes sure you can tell the difference.

sections.title: RFC Streams and Internet Standards
sections.content:
Users of RFCs should be aware that while all Internet Standards-related documents are published as RFCs, not all RFCs are Internet Standards-related documents. The IETF is responsible for maintaining the Internet Standards Process, which includes the requirements for developing, reviewing and approving Standards Track and Best Current Practice RFCs, and it also produces non-Standards-Track documents in the Informational, Experimental and Historic categories. Everything published as part of the IETF stream is reviewed by the appropriate IETF bodies.

Documents published in other streams are not generally reviewed by the IETF for things such as security, congestion control or inappropriate interaction with deployed protocols. They have also not been subject to approval by the Internet Engineering Steering Group, including an IETF-wide last call. The IETF therefore disclaims, for any non-IETF stream document, any knowledge of the fitness of that RFC for any purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a school library where some books were checked by the teachers and some were donated. The label tells you which kind you are holding.

sections.title: The Title Page Header
sections.content:
The information at the front of an RFC includes the names and affiliations of the authors and the publication month and year. Historically, a left-hand column carried the other header elements. The document source names the RFC stream. The old label Network Working Group is obsoleted for this purpose, and the possible entries are Internet Engineering Task Force, Internet Architecture Board, Internet Research Task Force and Independent Submission.

The Request for Comments element is the number assigned by the RFC Editor on publication. A subseries identifier and number appear for categories that have a subseries, currently Best Current Practices and STDs, and several RFCs may share one subseries number. An optional relation such as Updates or Obsoletes may be shown, and the category is always one of Standards Track, Best Current Practice, Experimental, Informational or Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the label on the front of a folder: who made it, its number, and what kind of document it is.

sections.title: The Status of This Memo
sections.content:
This section describes the category of the RFC, including the distribution statement, and it includes a statement about the stream-specific review of the material that clarifies the breadth and depth of review. It has three paragraphs. The first is a single sentence, clearly standing out, that identifies the stream-specific status, with the text defined by the stream and reviewed for clarity by the IAB and the RFC Series Editor.

The second paragraph describes the type of review and exposure the document has received, defined on a per-stream basis under the general review and oversight of the RFC Editor and IAB. The third paragraph points to where further relevant information can be found, which may include whether the RFC has been updated or obsoleted, its origin, a listing of possible errata, and how to give feedback. These paragraphs show only the initial status: a document can later change status to, for example, Historic, and this cannot be reflected in the document itself, only in the information the third paragraph refers to.
sections.plainLanguage: The first paragraph says what kind of paper this is, the second says who looked it over, and the third says where to check for news about it.

sections.title: Approved Status Texts
sections.content:
Appendix A holds the initial text for the IAB web page. For the first paragraph, a Standards Track document says that it is an Internet Standards Track document, and a Best Current Practice says that the memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice. Other categories say the document is not an Internet Standards Track specification and give a reason, such as informational purposes, the historical record, or examination, experimental implementation and evaluation.

The second paragraph depends on the stream and may open with a sentence specific to the category. For example, the Internet Architecture Board stream says the document is a product of the IAB and represents information the IAB deemed valuable for permanent record, while the Independent Submission text says the RFC Editor chose to publish the document at its discretion and makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment. For non-IETF streams a pointer to Section 2 of this RFC is added, saying such documents are not candidates for any level of Internet Standard. The RFC Editor maintains example expansions of all permutations of these paragraphs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a ready-made sentence for each kind of document, so every RFC of the same kind says the same thing in the same way.

sections.title: Other Elements and Editor Duties
sections.content:
RFCs carry other structural elements whose positioning and layout are the responsibility of the RFC Editor. These include a copyright notice with a reference to BCP 78 and an intellectual property statement referring to BCP 78 and BCP 79, whose content is defined by those BCPs, and an International Standard Serial Number, 2070-1721, which uniquely identifies the RFC series as a serial publication regardless of language or country, and has no significance beyond that identification. New elements may be introduced or obsoleted using a process consistent with RFC 4844.

The Security Considerations section is brief: misunderstanding the status of a memo could cause interoperability problems, and hence security and stability problems. The RFC Editor maintains an RFC Style Guide and is encouraged to show the stream in indices and interfaces as well as in the header.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the label, every RFC also has a copyright line and a serial number, a bit like a library book has a barcode.

data.title: RFC title page header
data.code:
<document source>                      <author name>
Request for Comments: <RFC number>     [<author affiliation>]
[<subseries ID> <subseries number>]    [more author info as appropriate]
[<RFC relation>:<RFC number[s]>]
Category: <category>
                                       <month year>

viz.caption: THE FOUR STREAMS NAMED IN THE HEADER (RFC 7841, SECTION 3.1)

items.title: Internet Engineering Task Force
items.text: The IETF stream; its documents are reviewed by the appropriate IETF bodies.

items.title: Internet Architecture Board
items.text: The IAB stream, representing information the IAB deems valuable for permanent record.

items.title: Internet Research Task Force
items.text: The IRTF stream, publishing the results of Internet-related research.

items.title: Independent Submission
items.text: Published at the RFC Editor's discretion, independently of any other stream.
